lesson.title: Running the Clock Backward: Antiderivatives and Definite Integrals
lesson.summary: Integration reverses differentiation, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus turns that reversal into a fast way to compute the exact area under a curve between two points.
lesson.body:
If a derivative tells you the rate of change of a function, an antiderivative asks the reverse question: given a rate of change, what was the original function? Finding an antiderivative means finding a function whose derivative matches the expression you started with. Because the derivative of any constant is zero, antiderivatives are never unique on their own, there's always a "+C" representing every possible constant that could have been present before differentiating, which is why an antiderivative found this way is called indefinite.

The basic rule for reversing the power rule is: to find the antiderivative of x^n, raise the exponent by one and divide by the new exponent, giving x^(n+1)/(n+1), valid whenever n does not equal -1. This is exactly the power rule for derivatives run backward, and you can always check an antiderivative is correct by differentiating it and confirming you land back on the original expression.

A definite integral, written ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx, represents the exact signed area between the curve y = f(x) and the x-axis, from x = a to x = b. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus connects this area directly to antiderivatives: if F(x) is any antiderivative of f(x), then ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). This theorem is what makes definite integrals computable by hand rather than requiring you to add up infinitely many infinitely thin rectangles by brute force, which is how the area is originally defined but not how it's practically calculated.

Here is a fully worked example. Evaluate ∫ from 1 to 3 of (3x² + 2) dx. First find an antiderivative: the antiderivative of 3x² is 3 × (x³/3) = x³, and the antiderivative of the constant 2 is 2x, so F(x) = x³ + 2x. Now apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus by evaluating F at the top limit and subtracting F at the bottom limit. At x = 3: F(3) = 3³ + 2(3) = 27 + 6 = 33. At x = 1: F(1) = 1³ + 2(1) = 1 + 2 = 3. Subtracting, F(3) - F(1) = 33 - 3 = 30. So the definite integral equals 30, meaning the area between the curve y = 3x² + 2 and the x-axis, from x = 1 to x = 3, is exactly 30 square units. This process, find an antiderivative, plug in the top limit, subtract the antiderivative evaluated at the bottom limit, is the single most important computational skill in integral calculus, and it sets up directly for finding areas between two curves rather than just between one curve and the x-axis.
